text: The story belongs to the boy in the corner, and the boy is only ever watching. Codine has served ten years for killing a friend, and what he comes back to in a turn-of-the-century Bucharest slum is a mother who counts her hoarded money in front of him and a child who has decided this is the man worth studying. Henri Colpi made it with French money and Romanian speech, and the imbalance suits the material: a neighbourhood where force is the only currency anyone has enough of, watched by someone still small enough to be told nothing. The film is not the ex-convict's biography. It is an education, and the lessons are accurate. Nothing in the frame suggests the poverty is temporary, and the adults behave accordingly, the miser guarding her coins and the strongman collecting what he believes he is owed.

Nearly everyone on screen is a celebrity of Chinese micro-blogs rather than an actor: a publisher, a folk singer, a screenwriter. Gao Qunshu built the film around them and around a real man, Zhang Huiling, a plainclothes policeman who has worked Shuangyushu, a community in Beijing's Haidian District, for more than ten years. What comes out is a crime picture pitched at the scale of a beat rather than a case, spent on ordinary people trying to hold their position in a very large city. The casting is the argument. People known for what they say online, put in front of a camera to play the metropolis they comment on, carry their own reputations into the frame with them, and the Golden Horse for best feature went to a film with almost no professional performers in it.

Two stories run at once here, and neither will let the other finish. One is eighteenth-century shogunate business: loyalty, obligation, men keeping careful accounts of what they owe. The other is a ghost story about a woman destroyed by passion and by the evil around her. Kinji Fukasaku braids the two, and the join is the interesting part, because the historical material insists that revenge is an order handed down and executed with discipline, while the supernatural material insists that nothing stays where the living put it. A hundred and six minutes carrying four genre labels at once, horror and drama and action and history, which is less a hedge than an accurate description of how it moves, changing register inside a scene and expecting both halves to be held at the same time.

Hitler gave him whatever budget he asked for and distrusted him anyway. Admiral Canaris ran the intelligence service of Nazi Germany, produced results with it, and made no secret of thinking the ideology beneath him, which left the party leadership uneasy without giving them much to act on. Made in 1954 and given the German Film Award for best feature, it arrives less than a decade after the war, and that date presses on every scene: a German audience handed a man who was inside the apparatus and not of it. Alfred Weidenmann keeps to offices and procedure rather than combat. Almost everything of consequence happens across a desk. The tension is conversational, a matter of what one official can risk saying aloud to another, and of how long a useful man stays useful.

Fog settles over Tempelhof and the planes stop, which leaves a terminal full of people who were supposed to be elsewhere by morning. Getting out of Berlin by other means turns out to be a genuine problem rather than an inconvenience, and Will Tremper builds his night out of that: separate passengers, separate predicaments, one building and one weather system holding them together. The comedy is arithmetical. The longer nobody can leave, the more each traveller has to rebuild a plan in front of strangers, and the less the airport resembles a place people merely pass through. The fog is impartial, and impartiality is a rare quality in a plot device, since it removes the same option from everyone at the same moment. What remains is a building full of people already sorted by where they were trying to go.

By the time the real trouble starts, the wrongful conviction is already over. Five years served for something he did not do, and then release, and then the talk: what his wife was doing while he was inside, with whom, how much of it is true. Hans W. Geißendörfer keeps the crime on a domestic scale, a marriage put under examination by a husband who has had five years to practise suspicion. Prison would be the obvious subject. Jealousy is the harder one, because it has no institution to blame and no release date, and because the man asking the questions does not want the answers he is fishing for. The film went to the Academy Awards as an international submission on the strength of a story that never leaves one marriage.

A romance sits inside a police procedural, and the film gives itself two hours and twelve minutes to hold both. The case is a killer who selects police officers as his targets, and the detective goes after him further than the job strictly requires. Yasuo Furuhata is not chiefly interested in the mechanics of the hunt, which the running time gives away: a thriller wanting only its plot would be an hour shorter. What fills the difference is the interval around the work. Waiting, travelling, the rooms a man passes through while the thing is unfinished. The romance is not a subplot bolted on, it is what those intervals fill up with. A pursuit carried that long stops being a chase and becomes a way of living, and the film appears to know which of the two it is filming.

In 1026, students in western China are seized and pushed into the army of Li Yuanhao, crown prince of Xi Xia, who intends to hold the trade road along its whole length. Zhao Xingde is one of them. He becomes the favourite of his commander, Zhu Wangli, which is at once a protection and a debt, and he is later sent off to learn the Xixian language, so the film has a scholar to follow as well as a soldier. Junya Satō spends two hours and twenty-three minutes the old way, on fortress walls and cavalry and distances that take real minutes to cross, and the largeness has a use. It makes Dun-Huang, the region's seat of learning, look like something a decision taken elsewhere could erase.

Every morning the old man walks down to the bus stop, and every evening he walks back without his son. Raghava Chakyar has a daughter's engagement to prepare for and a son, Raghu, who should have come home for it. What he learns is that the police took the boy for political reasons, and that finding out anything more will mean putting questions to people whose work is not to answer them. Shaji N. Karun moves at the pace of an old man's day, in Malayalam, and lets repetition do the pressing: the same road, the same hour, the same result. The National Film Award for best feature went to it. Nobody raises a voice, which is what makes the patience read less like resignation than like an accusation being filed very slowly.

A dam is being built, and the water will come to where Nagi's house stands. Three people live in it: Nagi, her husband, and a father-in-law who will not bend about how things are done. Girish Kasaravalli films in Kannada and mostly in one place, letting the domestic routine establish itself before the deadline starts eating into it, so that the flooding threatens a specific set of rooms and chores rather than an idea about home. Authority in the house belongs to the old man; the work of keeping it standing does not, and the film records that arrangement without comment, inside the ordinary sequence of a working day. Nagi's strength is shown as labour rather than as speech, which is the harder of the two to film.

Yasemin is seventeen, lives in Hamburg-Altona, and has parents who accept her German friends while expecting her to honour the traditions of the country they came from. The arrangement holds until Jan turns up, twenty-one and German and a student, at which point the two halves of it stop being compatible. Hark Bohm refuses to simplify either party. The parents are not drawn as an authority to be overthrown, and the daughter is not drawn as a case to be argued; both sides are trying to keep something they have every right to want. Germany sent the film to the Academy Awards as its international submission. What it does best is stay small, inside one household, where nobody gets to make a speech and everything turns on what people can bear to say to each other.

A father can keep his authority long after he has stopped being in the room. Buddhadeb Dasgupta hands that condition an entire film: a grown son in Bengal, his memory, and a parent whose size has not reduced with time. There is no investigation and no deadline, and recollection is the only engine, so everything rests on construction, on where the cuts fall and how long a shot is allowed to sit and what the film declines to explain. That is a demanding way to spend an hour and fifty-seven minutes. Nothing in it hurries to become an incident. It asks for the kind of attention given to a piece of music rather than to a plot, in which a figure comes back slightly altered and the alteration is the whole of the event.

Rajani's plan for her daughter is a marriage to a wealthy local businessman. Lati's plan is Calcutta. They live in the same brothel in a small Bengal town, and the gap between those two futures is the film: the mother has already priced the available options and believes she is being kind, while the daughter would rather take an unmapped road with the chance of an education somewhere at the end of it. Buddhadeb Dasgupta sends her out into a run of encounters with people who are strange in ways that have nothing to do with where she came from, which keeps the journey from hardening into a lesson. It holds the National Film Award for best Bengali feature. The argument it never states is that a risk chosen is not the same thing as a safety arranged.

The classroom belongs to a high school, but the students are adults and the hour is night. Yoji Yamada gives them a hundred and twenty-eight minutes and a teacher who is difficult company and worth the trouble, and fills the desks with people whom the ordinary route through Japanese schooling did not accommodate. A night school in a poor neighbourhood is a setting that invites sentiment. Yamada is aware of that and mostly declines the invitation. The length is the defence against it: at that duration the film has to find each student a separate reason for being in the room instead of one collective hardship, and the teacher cannot be the centre of every scene. What accumulates is less a story about a teacher than an attendance sheet with a life behind each name.
